newsitem.title: USA: Lake says Chinese missiles threaten U.S..
newsitem.headline: Lake says Chinese missiles threaten U.S..

text.p: President Bill Clinton's choice to be the next CIA director said on Thursday that Chinese missiles and missile-related sales posed a threat to the United States and U.S. interests abroad.

In a third day of often-testy Senate confirmation hearings that highlighted continued problems for his nomination, Lake was asked how he regarded China "in terms of their capabilities for threatening our country."
"I think they are real," Lake, Clinton's first-term national security adviser, said. "Certainly there is a missile threat from China."
"Certainly while in some areas our interests are similar, in many cases, they are not, and they work in ways that do not serve our interests ... and this is an extremely serious issue."
"Some of their activities on the proliferation side are damaging to our interests abroad in the Middle East and South Asia," he added in testimony before the Senate Intelligence Committee.

The United States has voiced concern over Chinese sales of missiles and related technology to Iran and Pakistan, possibly in violation of the Missile Technology Control Regime, a 31-nation pact designed to head off missile proliferation.

Lake was assailed during the session by Republican foes who impugned his integrity, management skills and fitness to head the troubled Central Intelligence Agency. The CIA has been rocked by treason in its ranks, frequent changes at the top and scandals in Guatemala and elsewhere.

The session heralded rough sledding for Lake on the Republican-controlled Senate floor, even assuming that two of the panel's 10 Republicans join the nine Democrats, as seems likely, to recommend confirmation by the full Senate.

Under questioning by Orrin Hatch, a Utah Republican, Lake said he was concerned by press reports that have linked Clinton friend James Riaddy of the Lippo Group, an Indonesia-based conglomerate, to alleged "front" companies for Chinese intelligence services. But he said he could not confirm the reports.

Lake stood by his previous refusal to condemn publicly two of his one-time National Security Council aides who failed to alert him about a June 1996 FBI warning on an alleged Chinese plan to buy influence with U.S. officeholders.

He confirmed that one of the two former subordinates, Edward Appel, had left his job after Clinton complained at a press conference on Monday that he should have been informed of the FBI's China concerns.

"I'm not sure whether he resigned or retired," Lake said of Appel, an FBI special agent assigned to the National Security Council. "And I certainly do not know whether it was related in any way" to the FBI briefing at issue.

The White House and the FBI did not return phone calls seeking clarification of Appel's departure, which came amid an extraordinary public rift between them over why the FBI information never made it up the chain of command.
Sen. James Inhofe, an Oklahoma Republican, took the nominee to task over Lake's stated exasperation at having his intellectual integrity called into question repeatedly.
"I really think you have mastered the art of righteous indignation during the course of this hearing," Inhofe told Lake.

Partisan feuding boiled over when Bob Graham, a Florida Democrat, complained that Republicans were spending too much time looking in the rear-view mirror rather than "out the windshield" and into the future.
"Sometimes you have to look in the rear view mirror to keep from being run over by a truck, Senator Graham, as you know," Committee Chairman Richard Shelby of Albama shot back.
